lead: A dual-fuel engine burns two fuels in one cycle: a gas that carries most of the energy, and a small diesel pilot that lights it. The reason is cetane. Methane and most gaseous fuels have a cetane number near zero, so air compressed to a diesel compression ratio will not ignite them in usable time; the pilot supplies the ignition. Multi-fuel means something different: one engine that runs on any one of several fuels, one at a time. You meet dual fuel in CNG buses, biogas gensets and LNG ships; multi-fuel in military trucks and farm engines.
prereq: You need: 6.6 for cetane, octane and calorific value, Unit 2 for injection and mixture preparation, and Unit 3 for ignition delay and knock.

sections.h3: Three words that are not synonyms

blocks.text: A dual-fuel engine burns two fuels in the same cycle, together. The gas carries most of the energy and the diesel is only the ignition source; both are inside the cylinder on every cycle.
A bi-fuel engine carries two fuels but burns one at a time. A CNG-petrol car is bi-fuel: a selector switches the fuel and the two never burn together.

A multi-fuel engine accepts any one of a range of single fuels, such as diesel, kerosene, a petrol blend or biodiesel, one at a time, without a hardware change at the roadside. Nothing burns together; the claim is fuel flexibility.

sections.h3: Metering the gas and lighting it

blocks.text: The gas is mixed with air before the intake valve. Three devices do it. A venturi mixer uses the pressure drop at a throat to draw gas in and hold the air-gas ratio roughly constant. A gas carburettor adds a zero-pressure regulator and a metering valve. Port injection puts solenoid injectors in the intake port and times the gas pulse, which gives better ratio control and less risk of a backfire in the manifold. Mixing gas into the intake air is called fumigation.

items: Gas is metered into the air in the intake, giving a lean premixed charge.
The charge is compressed. At a diesel compression ratio it is not hot enough, for long enough, for methane: a cetane number near zero means an ignition delay the cycle cannot wait for.
A small diesel pilot is injected near top dead centre.
The pilot burns first and its flame ignites the gas-air charge, then expansion follows as in a diesel.

blocks.text: Pilot size is quoted as a share of the total fuel energy, typically 5–30%. The share is small at high load, where the gas does the work, and large at light load, where a lean charge needs a bigger ignition source. Electronic common-rail injection sets the pilot mass per cycle accurately; a mechanical pump cannot.
A micro-pilot, a very small diesel injection that replaces the spark plug, ignites mixtures too lean for a spark in large-bore gas engines.

sections.h3: Substitution ratio, knock and the light-load penalty

blocks.where: ṁ_d is the diesel mass flow on diesel alone, in kg/h; ṁ_df is the diesel flow in dual-fuel mode, in kg/h; SR_mass is the fraction of diesel mass replaced.
ṁ_g is the gas mass flow, in kg/h; LHV_d and LHV_g are lower calorific values, in MJ/kg; SR_energy is the gas share of the fuel energy.

blocks.text: Knock in a dual-fuel engine appears at high load, where the substitution ratio is highest and the premixed charge is largest. If the pilot is advanced, the intake air hot or the compression ratio high, the end gas ignites before the flame front arrives. Methane's high octane number delays this, so knock is less of a limit than in a petrol engine, but it still caps the substitution at full load.

At light load the charge is very lean. Flame speed falls, some cycles burn incompletely, and CO and unburnt HC climb while efficiency drops (see 6.1). The unburnt methane leaving the cylinder is methane slip. It is natural gas itself, and it warms the climate far more per kg than CO2, so a few hundred ppm of slip matters more than the HC number suggests. Slip also comes from valve overlap, when fresh charge short-circuits to the exhaust.

A multi-fuel engine differs from a diesel in what the pump and the chamber can be told to do. Injection timing must follow cetane: a low-cetane fuel has a long ignition delay and needs advance. Compression ratio is fixed at build, so it is a compromise: high enough for reliable diesel ignition, but capped because the petrol-like fuels in the range knock at high compression. Boost and nozzle size are matched to the fuel's calorific value and viscosity.

Four properties set the fuel range. Cetane decides whether the fuel ignites at all. Viscosity sets the spray and the pump's internal leakage. Lubricity protects pump and injector from wear. Volatility matters for petrol blends, which can vapour-lock a hot pump.

One example: some military trucks used a multifuel diesel with a density compensator on the distributor pump, which trims the injected volume as fuel density changes, so one setting works for diesel, kerosene and petrol blends.

Producer gas is made by burning wood, rice husk or charcoal in a restricted air supply; it is mostly CO and H2, with a calorific value several times lower than natural gas per unit volume. A producer-gas engine is therefore derated, and the diesel pilot share stays higher than with CNG. This is the classic rural off-grid set: gasifier, diesel engine, village load.
In shipping, dual fuel means LNG with a small pilot in a large two-stroke or four-stroke engine. At full load the pilot is a very small energy share; the penalty is methane slip, not diesel use.

examples.question: A dual-fuel engine runs at 40 kW. On diesel alone it burns 10 kg/h. In dual-fuel mode it burns 2.5 kg/h of diesel (LHV 42.5 MJ/kg) and 5.5 kg/h of CNG (LHV 50 MJ/kg). Find the substitution by mass and the gas share of the fuel energy.
steps: Energy rate on diesel alone = 10 kg/h × 42.5 MJ/kg = 425 MJ/h.
Diesel energy rate in dual-fuel mode = 2.5 kg/h × 42.5 MJ/kg = 106.25 MJ/h.
Gas energy rate = 5.5 kg/h × 50 MJ/kg = 275 MJ/h.
Gas share of energy = 275 ÷ 381.25 = 0.7213, that is 72.1%. Diesel share = 100 − 72.1 = 27.9%.
examples.answer: 75% of the diesel mass is replaced, and the gas supplies 72.1% of the fuel energy while the diesel supplies 27.9%.
examples.check:
m_d = 10.0
m_df = 2.5
m_g = 5.5
L_d = 42.5
L_g = 50.0
sub_mass = (m_d - m_df) / m_d * 100
E_alone = m_d * L_d
E_d = m_df * L_d
E_g = m_g * L_g
E_tot = E_d + E_g
share_g = E_g / E_tot * 100
share_d = E_d / E_tot * 100
print(round(sub_mass, 1))
print(round(E_alone, 2))
print(round(E_d, 2))
print(round(E_g, 2))
print(round(E_tot, 2))
print(round(share_g, 1))
print(round(share_d, 1))

traps: Quoting substitution by mass when the question asks for the share of energy. The two calorific values differ, so 75% by mass becomes 72.1% by energy here.
Calling a CNG-petrol car a dual-fuel engine. It is bi-fuel: the fuels are switched, never burnt together.
Treating the pilot as a fixed 10%. The pilot is a share of energy set per operating point; it is large at light load and small at high load.
Assuming more substitution is always better. At light load it brings misfire, CO, HC and methane slip; at high load it brings knock.

Confusing methane slip with the HC limit. Slip is unburnt methane, counted as HC, but each kg warms the climate far more than a kg of CO2, so a small HC number still matters. It comes from incomplete or missed combustion of the lean charge, and from fresh charge short-circuiting to the exhaust during valve overlap.

quiz.q: Define a dual-fuel engine in one sentence.
quiz.a: An engine in which a gaseous fuel carrying most of the energy is burnt together with a small diesel pilot that provides ignition, every cycle.
An engine that carries two fuels and runs on one at a time, switched by a selector, such as a CNG-petrol car.

quiz.q: Why will methane not run a diesel engine of compression ratio 17 on its own?
quiz.a: Methane has a cetane number close to zero, so the compressed air temperature gives an ignition delay too long for the cycle; a diesel pilot supplies a local high-temperature ignition source instead.

quiz.q: An engine on diesel alone burns 8 kg/h. In dual-fuel mode it burns 2 kg/h of diesel (LHV 42.5 MJ/kg) and 4 kg/h of gas (LHV 50 MJ/kg). Find the substitution by mass and the gas share of energy.
quiz.a: Mass: (8 − 2) ÷ 8 = 0.75, that is 75%. Energies: diesel alone 8 × 42.5 = 340 MJ/h; dual diesel 85 MJ/h; gas 200 MJ/h; total 285 MJ/h. Gas share = 200 ÷ 285 = 70.2%; diesel 29.8%.

quiz.q: Why does dual-fuel efficiency fall at light load but knock appear at high load?
quiz.a: At light load the premixed charge is very lean, flame speed is low and some cycles burn incompletely, so CO, HC and methane slip rise and efficiency drops. At high load the substitution is high, so a large premixed charge is compressed with a hot end gas and auto-ignites before the flame arrives, which is knock.

quiz.q: Name three fuel properties that limit the fuel range of a multi-fuel engine and say what each affects.
quiz.a: Cetane, which sets ignition delay; viscosity, which sets spray quality and pump leakage; lubricity, which sets pump and injector wear.

quiz.q: A dual-fuel engine at 25% load shows high CO and high CH4 in the exhaust. Suggest two changes and justify each.
quiz.a: Increase the diesel pilot share and reduce gas substitution, so the charge is less lean and burns more completely; raise the intake charge temperature or reduce the excess air, so flame speed and completeness improve. Retarding or advancing the pilot slightly can also help, but the main lever is the gas-diesel ratio.

beyond: Not for the exam. LNG dual fuel is the practical bridge in shipping, and methanol and ammonia dual-fuel engines are being introduced because a low-cetane liquid needs the same pilot idea. The International Maritime Organization's greenhouse gas strategy counts methane slip as an emission, so pilot strategy and slip measurement are active work. Producer-gas dual fuel remains a live rural electrification option where biomass is cheap and the grid is not.
